On the night of Ramchandra Ray’s escape, Udayaditya was the active one: he drew his sword, commanded Sitaram to open the door, disarmed him, and tied him up with his own cloth. Sitaram submitted, folded his hands, took the dust from Udayaditya’s feet, and asked Udayaditya to bind him. On the night of Udayaditya’s own escape from prison, the roles reverse: Sitaram enters the dark room, says the prison is on fire, grabs Udayaditya and almost carries him out, tells him “Come, come with me,” and Udayaditya helplessly asks, “What should I do? Where should I go?” and follows Sitaram’s lead.

Pratapaditya initially ordered two Pathan men to kill Basanta Ray when he took shelter at the inn in Simultali on his way to Jessore; this failed because the Pathan could not bring himself to do it. Finally, Muktiyar Khan carried out Pratapaditya’s signed death sentence, and Abdul killed Basanta Ray with a drawn sword.
At Jessore’s inner quarters, disguised as a middle-aged woman; and at Chandradwip’s palace, in his jester’s guise.
The Mahishi secretly had Matangini fetch medicine from Mangala, who prepared a poison; Surma then took poison and died.
Her husband, the Maharaj, married another woman, so when Vibha finally arrived there was no place for her in her own kingdom or royal palace, and all her hopes of happiness were shattered.

Rukmini got Udayaditya’s signet ring from him, and Sitaram and Bhagavat used its seal to stamp a forged petition pretending Udayaditya was plotting treason against Pratapaditya with the Emperor. Bhagavat then brought the petition to Pratapaditya, and it was used as evidence that caused Pratapaditya to order Udayaditya’s imprisonment.

After Ramchandra Ray’s midnight escape, Pratapaditya dismissed Sitaram and Bhagavat. When Udayaditya learned of Sitaram’s poverty, he began giving monthly stipends to Sitaram and Bhagavat. Pratapaditya forbade this, so Surma secretly took over sending the stipends through a trusted maid. The maid told Mangala, and word reached Pratapaditya. As a result, Pratapaditya ordered that Surma must go to her paternal home.

The song expresses Basanta Ray’s loneliness, grief, and sense of emptiness after those he loved and sang for are gone; singing no longer brings him joy because he is left behind alone. He first sings it in Raigarh, alone on his palace veranda at sunset, humming to himself as he longs for absent loved ones. He later sings it in Jessore, in the silent, empty inner quarters after Vibha tells him no one is there; taking Vibha’s hand, he slowly begins to sing it as the room seems to cry that those who were there before are there no more.

Because Rukmini failed to stop Udayaditya’s midnight escape, Udayaditya got away with Basanta Ray to Raigarh. Rukmini then told Pratapaditya that the Yubaraj had escaped with the old king of Raigarh and that Sitaram, the old king, and Udayaditya had conspired. Pratapaditya sent men with Rukmini, learned that Udayaditya was in Raigarh, and then gave Muktiyar Khan a secret order: the death sentence for the King of Raigarh. Muktiyar Khan carried out the order, and Basanta Ray was killed.

Pratapaditya initially received Ramchandra coolly and without joy or haste, treated him as a subordinate son-in-law, and made him feel Pratapaditya’s superiority. Later, in Ramchandra’s own court, Ramchandra allowed and enjoyed daily ridicule of Pratapaditya, portrayed him as inferior, and had his courtiers mock and tear down Pratapaditya’s status while exalting himself as greater.

The older widow from Raigarh was Rukmini. She later left Raigarh, changed her name to Mangala, and lived on the outskirts of Jessore. After befriending palace servants and learning palace news, she was secretly sent for by the Rajmahishi to prepare medicine to win back Udayaditya’s heart from Surma. Instead, Mangala spent five days preparing a poison with mantras so that Udayaditya would feel no pity when Surma died. Surma then died after taking poison, and the palace believed she had taken her own life, causing tragedy in Jessore.

Udayaditya’s early lament that he was unfit to be crown prince and wished he had not been born heir culminates when he is brought before Pratapaditya as a prisoner. Pratapaditya tells him he is not worthy of the kingdom, and Udayaditya agrees, asking to be released from the throne. To prove his sincerity, he goes to the temple and takes an oath before Ma-Kali that he will never accept even an iota of the kingdom of Jessore, will not sit on its throne, and will not touch its royal scepter; Samaraditya is declared heir. He then renounces kingdom and family and leaves for Kashi as an ascetic.

Nayanchand, instead of delivering the letter to Pratapaditya, gave it to the Mahishi. The Mahishi hid it, showed it to Basanta Ray, and on his advice announced throughout the household—and thus to Vibha—that Ramchandra Ray had written a letter requesting that Vibha be sent to Chandradwip, though the letter actually said he had renounced her and she should not be sent there again.

Pratapaditya blocked the canal with large sal-wood logs, but Rammohan and his followers pulled the boat up and over the logs, while the guards’ stones fell short and their attempt to chase by boat was delayed, so Ramchandra Ray escaped.

Basanta Ray’s sitar, once his “eternal companion,” becomes a sign of his despair: when parting from Udayaditya he leaves it behind and says he will not play it anymore, his playing already hindered by tears; later he no longer has it with him, says its strings have broken and it can no longer be tuned, and his singing holds no joy because those he loved are gone. Finally, when he hears Udayaditya is imprisoned, he is startled, stops singing, and cries out, “Dada, come to me!”—showing that without Udayaditya his music and joy have collapsed into grief.

Earlier, Udayaditya was known to involve himself in the affairs of the subjects and act against Pratapaditya’s wishes; he would stop an official without considering consequences and try to protect the oppressed. After Surma’s death, his former courage was gone, he became extremely afraid of Pratapaditya, hesitated in every task, and no longer had the courage to intervene: he called for his horse but then went nowhere, ran inside upon seeing a subject beaten, and failed to help Bhagavat and Sitaram.
He rescues Udayaditya from the prison during the fire: Sitaram opens the prison door, tells him the prison is on fire, pulls him out, and leads him away to freedom.

On the first occasion, Rammohan tied Ramchandra Ray to his back, climbed down a rope made from twisted bedsheets from the palace roof, gripped the rope with his teeth at the end, released Ramchandra, lowered him carefully with both hands into the boat, and then jumped down himself. On the second occasion, after Vibha fainted, Rammohan lifted her and carried her out of the palace, placed her into a palanquin near the gate, and returned to the boat.

In Jessore, Vibha is elaborately adorned by the Mahishi with eight thick gold bangles and a huge diamond bracelet on each arm, a large nose ring, and a styled coiffure, carrying the burden of ornaments and a joyous, shy face. In Chandradwip, she refuses a palanquin, says she will go “like a common subject, like a beggar-woman,” dresses as a common woman, enters the palace like any other maidservant with no welcome, and is mistaken by the king for a beggar woman seeking alms.

In his bedchamber after Surma’s death, the window symbolizes Surma’s absence and his lingering hope of seeing her there; he sits by it amid the same moonlight, garden, and breeze, feeling that she should not be gone. In the prison cell, the small window instead symbolizes freedom and liberation: Udayaditya sits near it to see the sky, birds, bamboo grove, and Shiva temple, and through it he believes his cage will one day break and he will be free; away from it he sees only darkness and feels imprisoned.

Their relationship begins as a flirtatious financial arrangement: Rukmini lends money at interest, while Sitaram is drawn to both her beauty and her silver. He borrows money, flatters her as “Subhadra,” “Pranpriye,” and the like, promises repayment tomorrow, but his memory of the debt vanishes; he visits often and they confer secretly. After Udayaditya is imprisoned, Sitaram turns on Rukmini, cursing her and threatening to set her house on fire and ruin her unless he frees the Yubaraj. Rukmini is enraged because the Yubaraj is hers too, and she alone can help or harm him. Later, when Sitaram thinks Mangala is dead and enters her cottage to take her money, he finds her alive, wet, ashen, and seemingly returned from Yama. She threatens to lay him and the Yubaraj in the oven and smear herself with ash from their pyres. He feigns affection; she becomes more enraged, searches for a curved blade to kill him, and he slips out while she strikes the floor where he had stood. She then denounces him to Pratapaditya, and he flees Jessore.

The guardhouse fire first served as a distraction: when the alarm spread, the guards ran from Udayaditya’s door, and Sitaram entered the dark prison and carried Udayaditya out. It then became a cover-up when Sitaram’s men kept the firefighting confused, set fire to Udayaditya’s now-empty prison cell, and Sitaram threw bones, a skull, and Udayaditya’s sword into the room. He spread shouts that the Yubaraj’s cell had caught fire, that he had been heard screaming, and that the roof had collapsed. This made it appear that Udayaditya had died in the fire, so the escape was hidden behind a false death.

He did not feel gratitude; he believed Udayaditya had saved him only for his sister’s sake, not out of concern for Ramchandra, and in his court he brought up Udayaditya’s name to laugh and joke about him without care, as if Udayaditya’s only crime was being Pratapaditya’s son.

The Emperor of Delhi was first dismissed by Pratapaditya as an empty threat whose name he would not even hear. Later, Bhagavat and Sitaram forged a petition, sealed with Udayaditya’s seal, pretending that Udayaditya was lodging a complaint of treason against Pratapaditya with the Emperor of Delhi in order to gain the kingdom. Bhagavat brought this petition to Pratapaditya instead of Delhi, making it appear that his son was betraying him to the Emperor. This forged petition to the Emperor became the mechanism by which Udayaditya was imprisoned.

In Surma’s presence, Vibha secretly went to Surma and had her hair done to her own liking, so Surma’s care and intervention were marked in Vibha’s coiffure. After Surma is gone, Vibha sits quietly at the time for braiding her hair, as if waiting for Surma to come and braid it, but evening and night come and Surma does not; her hair remains unbraided. Later, Rammohan sees that Vibha’s hair is unkempt, showing there is no one left to care for her.
